steps: Close your dominant hand, leaving the index finger extended straight upward.
Hold the extended fingertip against the side of your chin, close to the jawline.
Brush the finger along your chin, moving from your dominant side across to the other side.
Keep the finger pointing upward and the palm angled toward your face through the brush.
Mouth the word 'son' clearly, since the sign shares its handshape with 'boy'.
tip: The sign for SON shares its hand movement with BOY — the lip pattern tells them apart.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand relaxed in front of you, palm facing sideways.
Shape your dominant hand with the index finger and thumb pinched together.
Slide the pinched fingers up the ring finger of your non-dominant hand.
Move slowly from the knuckle toward the fingertip, as if fitting a wedding ring.
Smile gently and mouth 'wife', since the same sign also covers husband and spouse.
tip: One sign covers wife, husband and spouse — mouthing picks the English word.

steps: Extend the index and middle fingers of your dominant hand, closing the rest into a fist.
Hold the hand at chest height in front of your body, fingers pointing upward.
Glide the hand sideways to one side, then back again, in a small smooth motion.
Repeat the sideways glide two or three times, as if indicating two people.
Keep your palm facing forward and your expression neutral and inclusive.
tip: Fingerspelling M then F (mother, father) is the older form; the two-finger version suits any parents.

steps: Pinch the fingertips and thumb of your dominant hand together into a bunched shape.
Bring the bunched hand up toward your mouth, fingertips pointing inward.
Touch the fingertips lightly to your lips, as if placing food into your mouth.
Repeat the touch once more with the same small, crisp motion.
Keep your palm facing sideways and look toward your hand as you sign.
tip: The bunched-hand-to-mouth motion is shared with 'eat' — context and mouthing decide.

steps: Curve the fingers and thumb of your dominant hand into a C, like holding a small cup.
Lift the C hand to chin height in front of your mouth.
Tilt your wrist back and forth repeatedly, as if sipping from a cup.
Keep the motion gentle and rhythmic, with two or three easy tilts.
Mouth 'coffee' to fix the drink, since cup shares this handshape.
tip: The C-hand sipping motion is shared with cup; mouthing names the one you mean.

steps: Curve the fingers and thumb of your dominant hand into a C shape.
Raise the C hand to mouth height, as if holding a cup in your hand.
Tilt the hand back slightly toward your lips, as if taking a sip.
Repeat the small tilt once or twice with an easy, even rhythm.
Mouth the word 'cup' clearly, since coffee shares this sipping motion.
tip: Cup and coffee use the same C-hand sipping motion; your mouth pattern names the one you mean.

steps: Extend the index and middle fingers of both hands, keeping each pair together.
Point both finger-pairs downward in front of your body at chest height.
Bounce both hands up and down together in small, quick movements.
Keep the bounce lively, repeating two or three playful beats.
Smile as you sign — dog is a cheerful, bouncy sign.
tip: Two bouncing finger-pairs are the dog's legs on the move — keep the bounce small and quick.

steps: Curl the fingers of both hands into claw shapes, thumbs held out.
Hold both clawed hands in front of your chest, palms angled downward.
Circle the hands forward in repeated round motions.
Keep the circles smooth and even, two or three full loops.
Keep your gaze forward — the looping claws suggest all kinds of creatures.
tip: The generic ANIMAL sign is a catch-all; name the specific animal after it for clarity.

steps: Close both hands into fists and stack one on top of the other.
Hold the stacked hands in front of your body at waist height.
Move the hands up and down together, as if holding a pair of reins.
Keep the movement small and steady, like gentle tugs on the reins.
Lean slightly forward with an alert expression, as if riding.
tip: You are holding invisible reins — the up-down tugs name the horse.

steps: Open your dominant hand fully, fingers together and thumb relaxed.
Hold the open hand out in front of you at waist height.
Push the hand forward while twisting your wrist from side to side.
Keep the twists small and repeated, like a fish wriggling forward.
Point your fingertips forward so the hand glides like a swimming fish.
tip: The wriggling wrist is the fish's tail — mouth 'fish' when you mean it as food.

steps: Curl the fingers of both hands into claw shapes, thumbs tucked in.
Touch the fingertips of both clawed hands to your cheeks.
Drag both hands outward from your cheeks in one smooth pull.
End with the hands slightly apart at face width, palms angled outward.
Narrow your eyes slightly, as if picturing the whiskers you traced.
tip: You are pulling a cat's whiskers outward from the cheeks — two quick drags work too.

steps: Close your non-dominant hand into a fist and hold it steady.
Lay your flat dominant hand on top of the fist, palm facing down.
Stroke the dominant hand forward over the fist, as if petting an animal.
Repeat the stroke a second time with the same gentle motion.
Keep your face soft and warm — you are stroking a small animal.
tip: You are literally stroking a small animal — the mime is the sign.

steps: Close your dominant hand into a firm fist.
Place the fist against the side of your cheek.
Brush the fist downward and slightly forward along your cheek.
Make the stroke short and definite, once only.
Keep the fist closed through the stroke — an open hand changes the sign.
tip: One firm downward brush of the fist — night darkening over the face.

steps: Extend the index finger of your dominant hand, closing the other fingers.
Touch the fingertip to one side of your lower lip.
Sweep the finger along the lower lip toward the opposite side.
Repeat the sweep once or twice with a light, easy motion.
Mouth 'red' as you sign — the lips are busy in this one.
tip: Some signers swipe downward on the lip instead of across; the lower lip is the constant.

steps: Hold your non-dominant arm in front of you with the palm facing up.
Open your dominant hand flat, fingers held together.
Rest the flat dominant hand lightly on the upturned wrist.
Rub in small circles, keeping the wrist movement controlled and local.
Keep the circles tight on the wrist rather than up the forearm.
tip: Blue rubs circles on the wrist — green slides along the forearm instead.

steps: Hold your non-dominant arm in front of your body, palm facing down.
Shape your dominant hand into a closed flat hand, fingers together.
Slide the dominant hand along the top of your forearm toward the elbow.
Flick the hand upward as you reach the elbow, in one smooth finish.
Keep the sliding contact light — you are brushing the arm, not pressing.
tip: Blue circles the wrist; green slides the forearm — the location names the colour.

steps: Form the BSL fingerspelled letter G with your dominant hand.
Hold both hands in front of your chest, starting with the fingers closed.
Move both hands apart sideways while opening the fingers outward.
Make the opening bright and expansive, like spreading a treasure.
Mouth 'gold' to separate it from yellow, which signs up at the head.
tip: G gives the initial, the opening hands give the glitter.

steps: Touch your middle fingertip to your thumb, forming a small circle.
Raise the hand to the side of your head at temple height.
Flick the middle finger outward against the thumb, repeatedly.
Keep the flicks quick and light, two or three in a steady rhythm.
Keep your palm facing forward as the finger flicks.
tip: The repeated flick beside the head is yellow — one flick reads differently.

steps: Curl your dominant hand into a claw shape, fingers spread.
Place the clawed hand against the inside of your non-dominant elbow.
Drag the clawed hand along the underside of your forearm toward the wrist.
Keep the drag smooth and continuous in one steady stroke.
Hold the non-dominant arm still and relaxed throughout.
tip: BSL SignBank documents regional variants of BROWN; the forearm-drag form is the most widely taught.
